description: Historic 19th-century cafe known for Neapolitan coffee and pastries, a beloved meeting place for locals and artists:contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}.
Historic pastry shop (est. 1830) by Amalfi’s cathedral, famed for traditional pastries like the Delizia al Limone and chocolate-dipped scorzette:contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}.
Historic café (est. 1892) run by the Assenza family, renowned for its artisanal Sicilian pastries, granita, and gelato made with local citrus:contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}.
Legendary pastry shop famous for its convent-inspired almond sweets and marzipan, founded by Maria Grammatico and set in a charming courtyard:contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}.

Historic cafe on Lecce’s main piazza Sant’Oronzo, known for its rustico leccese (savory puff pastry) and custard-filled pasticciotto enjoyed with views of Roman ruins:contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}.

Family-run pastry shop credited with inventing the pasticciotto in 1745 – a custard-filled shortcrust tart – still made by the Ascalone family in their tiny historic bakery:contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}.

Historic café founded in 1801, a fixture in Cosenza’s old town where generations have gathered for coffee. Famous for its own anise liqueur and almond sweets like the “varchiglia”:contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}:contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}.
Iconic Palermo pastry shop known for its rich Setteveli chocolate-hazelnut cake, cannoli, and classic Sicilian desserts, often hailed among the city’s best sweet spots.

Chic open-air cocktail bar with spectacular views of Positano and the sea, serving classic and creative drinks in a stylish terrace setting (famous for its sunset atmosphere):contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}.

Rustic village bar featured in *The Godfather*, offering refreshing granita and local wine on a vine-covered terrace in the quiet medieval piazza of Savoca:contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}:contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}.

Quirky multi-level bar famed for its cheeky phallic-themed decor and panoramic views over Taormina and Mt. Etna. A Castelmola institution since 1947, also known for house-made almond wine:contentReference[oaicite:11]{index=11}:contentReference[oaicite:12]{index=12}.

Capri’s legendary late-night tavern with live music and dancing. A celebrity hotspot where local bands and patrons sing Italian classics into the early morning in a lively, tambourine-shaking atmosphere.

Award-winning craft cocktail bar in Lecce’s historic center, tucked in a vaulted stone alcove. Renowned for expert mixologists who shake up inventive cocktails in a cool, laid-back environment:contentReference[oaicite:13]{index=13}.

Trendy multi-functional lounge in Matera’s Sassi district that doubles as a cocktail bar, casual eatery, and arts venue. Popular for creative signature drinks and DJ sets under its cave-like tuff stone ceiling:contentReference[oaicite:14]{index=14}.
Intimate speakeasy-style bar in Naples (often ranked among the world’s top bars) known for its sophisticated vintage ambiance and impeccably crafted classic cocktails using premium spirits.

Elegant open-air lounge bar in Capri with modern chic decor and breathtaking views of the Faraglioni rocks and marina. Specializes in champagne and craft cocktails, perfect for a luxurious sunset drink.

World-renowned two-Michelin-star restaurant and boutique inn offering refined Mediterranean cuisine rooted in Campanian tradition. The Iaccarino family’s iconic establishment, celebrated for its organic farm-to-table ingredients and exquisite tasting menus:contentReference[oaicite:15]{index=15}.

Romantic Michelin-starred restaurant in Positano’s Le Sirenuse Hotel. Illuminated by hundreds of candles each evening, it serves elegant Amalfi Coast cuisine with fresh local seafood and herbs, accompanied by mandolin serenades:contentReference[oaicite:16]{index=16}.

Exclusive two-Michelin-star restaurant tucked in the bay of Nerano. Chef Antonio Mellino crafts inventive seafood-centric tasting menus (including the famous spaghetti with zucchini) paired with wines from an extensive cellar in a chic coastal setting.

Chef Ciccio Sultano’s two-Michelin-star restaurant in Ragusa Ibla – a standard-bearer for Sicilian haute cuisine:contentReference[oaicite:17]{index=17}. Serves imaginative interpretations of Sicilian flavors (like Modica chocolate or local tuna) in an elegant baroque-palazzo setting.

Chef Pino Cuttaia’s intimate two-Michelin-star restaurant in Licata, where Sicilian culinary memories are transformed into modern fine dining:contentReference[oaicite:18]{index=18}. Known for signature dishes like \Cloud of Mozzarella\" and aromatic seafood couscous that reinvent tradition."

Dramatic fine dining restaurant set inside a natural sea cave on the Adriatic. Offers a unique romantic experience dining by candlelight above the waves, with upscale Apulian-inspired dishes and fresh seafood in a one-of-a-kind atmosphere (premium pricing applies).

Lecce’s first Michelin-starred restaurant run by a young avant-garde team. Offers an experimental tasting menu that playfully deconstructs and reimagines Apulian ingredients in a minimalist, edgy dining space – a polarizing but unforgettable culinary experience.

Stylish one-Michelin-star restaurant tucked in Calabria’s Aspromonte mountains. Chef Nino Rossi’s creative cuisine shines here, spotlighting wild local ingredients (like bergamot, wild mushrooms) in artful dishes that redefine Calabrian tradition in a serene rural setting.

Perhaps Naples’ most famous pizzeria (est. 1870), known as the “sacred temple of pizza”:contentReference[oaicite:19]{index=19}. Serves only two varieties – Margherita and Marinara – but their perfect wood-fired crust and simple fresh toppings inspire daily lines out the door.

Legendary pizzeria on Via dei Tribunali in Naples. Gino Sorbillo’s pies feature a soft, chewy crust and balanced toppings, earning worldwide acclaim. Expect a lively crowd and long waits for arguably one of the city’s best pizzas.

No-frills, boisterous trattoria in Naples’ Spanish Quarter serving hearty home-style Neapolitan classics (like pasta e patate, fried anchovies) at low prices. The theatrical waiters and communal tables make dining here a fun, authentic local experience.

Family-run seaside restaurant in Marina del Cantone, Nerano, reachable partly by boat. Revered for its ultra-fresh seafood and famous spaghetti alla nerano (zucchini pasta). Casual ambiance on a pier; a favorite of food lovers and celebrities seeking rustic charm.

Rustic farmhouse restaurant perched high above Positano. Offers no menu – just abundant fixed-course meals of whatever is freshly harvested and cooked that day. Guests enjoy sweeping views, grilled meats, garden vegetables, house wine, and warm family hospitality.

Historic eatery (est. 1834) in Palermo famous for traditional Sicilian street foods. Locals flock here for **pane ca’ meusa** (spleen sandwiches), panelle (chickpea fritters) and arancine in an atmospheric, old-world setting that’s part restaurant, part street stall.

Celebrated countryside osteria in rural Puglia run by chef Pietro Zito. A pioneer of farm-to-table dining, it serves rustic Apulian dishes made from ingredients grown in its own gardens (homemade bread, foraged herbs, local olive oil) in a cozy, unpretentious setting.

Atmospheric trattoria built into a stone cave in Matera’s Sassi district. Specializes in hearty Lucanian cuisine such as homemade orecchiette with tomato sauce, pezzente sausage, and crispy peperoni cruschi. Candle-lit grotto setting provides a historic charm.

Popular pizzeria and friggitoria on Via Tribunali known for its street food. Famed for its fried delights like arancini and frittatine, alongside classic wood-fired pizzas you can fold and eat on the go – even Bill Clinton stopped here for a slice in 1994.

Tiny street-food stall in Naples specializing in **'o cuoppo**, the paper cone of mixed fried goodies. Serves piping hot bites like calamari, shrimp, mozzarella bites and zucchini blossoms – a quintessential Neapolitan snack to enjoy while strolling.

Hole-in-the-wall bakery in Bari Vecchia famed for its focaccia barese. Locals and tourists line up for squares of oily, crunchy-edged focaccia topped with tomatoes, olives, and oregano – arguably the tastiest (and cheapest) lunch in town, fresh from the oven.

Family-owned cheese shop and deli stand in the Ortigia market, world-famous for its colossal made-to-order panini. The cheerful Borderi family stacks local cheeses, cured meats, veggies, and sauces into epic sandwiches – an entertaining show and a delicious bargain meal.

Unassuming deli near Capri’s Marina Grande that has achieved cult status for its simple yet sublime sandwiches. Fresh baked bread stuffed with mozzarella, prosciutto, tomato, basil and a drizzle of olive oil – the perfect beach picnic, often enjoyed right on the pier.

Hidden gem in Palermo: a tiny, centuries-old fry shop tucked in an alley, selling bite-sized arancine, meatballs, timballetti and other fritti. A classic stop for authentic Palermitano street finger food, still wrapped in paper and perfect for an on-the-go nibble.

Trendy fast-casual spot that originated in Polignano, known for its gourmet seafood sandwiches. Offers creative Apulian street food like octopus burgers, tuna tartare rolls, and fried fish cones. Popular with the Instagram crowd – expect a line during peak hours.

Historic gelato shop by Reggio’s seafront (in business for over a century). Famous for its bergamot gelato made from local Calabrian citrus, along with a variety of classic and innovative flavors. A must-stop for a refreshing cone while strolling the Lungomare Falcomatà.
